title: The order annihilates a finite commutative group scheme
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and let $G$ be a finite commutative $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme]. Put $n=\dim_k\Gamma(G,\mathcal O_G)$, its order. Then $n\geq1$, and for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$ and every $x\in G(R)$ one has $n x=0$. Equivalently the scheme morphism obtained by adding the identity morphism of $G$ to itself $n$ times is the zero homomorphism. No reducedness, etaleness or invertibility of $n$ in $k$ is assumed.

source.place: Proposition 11.32, printed p.221, restricted to commutative finite group schemes; n is positive because the identity section makes the coordinate algebra nonzero.

proof.text: Write $A=\Gamma(G,\mathcal O_G)$, finite-dimensional by [def-sc-group-scheme]. The identity gives a unital $k$-algebra map $\epsilon:A\to k$, so $A\ne0$ and $n\geq1$. Choose an algebraic closure $K/k$ by [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], $G_K$ has coordinate algebra $A\otimes_kK$. It suffices to prove the equality of the multiplication-by-$n$ and zero maps after extending scalars to $K$: a $k$-basis of $A$ becomes a $K$-basis of $A\otimes_kK$, hence the dimension stays $n$ and the map $A\to A\otimes_kK$, $a\mapsto a\otimes1$, is injective. Equality of the extended coordinate maps therefore implies equality of the original ones. The scalar extension uses [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. From now on replace $k$ by $K$.

Apply [lem-sfb-finite-commutative-group-local-constant-product] to write $G\simeq C\times_KH_K$ with $C$ connected, $B=\Gamma(C,\mathcal O_C)$ local, $I=\ker(\epsilon:B\to K)$ its maximal ideal, $d=\dim_KB\geq1$, $q=|H|\geq1$ and $n=dq$. By [lem-sfb-finite-additive-group-card-annihilator], $[q]$ vanishes on $H$. Thus it vanishes on the constant group scheme $H_K$: on each component $\operatorname{Spec}K$ it is the map labelled $qh=0$. Consequently $[n]=[d]\circ[q]$ vanishes there as well. It remains to prove $[d]=0$ on $C$.

In characteristic zero, $C$ is etale by the characteristic-zero clause of [lem-sc-fg-order-prime-etale]. Its finite coordinate algebra is a product of finite separable extensions of $K$ by [lem-sc-finite-etale-algebra-criterion]. Each factor equals $K$ because $K$ is algebraically closed. As $B$ is nonzero local, this product has exactly one factor. Hence $B=K$, $C=\operatorname{Spec}K$ is the trivial group, $d=1$ and $[d]=0$.

Suppose instead that $K$ has positive characteristic $p$. A finite group scheme over a field is flat since its coordinate algebra is a vector space and thus free. Apply [lem-sc-connected-finite-order] to the connected finite flat group scheme $C$: there is $r\geq0$ with $d=p^r$.

We have $I^d=0$. Indeed each $I^j$ is finite as a $B$-module: a finite $K$-basis also generates it over $B$. If $I^{j+1}=I^j$, apply [lem-weil-pbc-nakayama-jacobson] to $M=I^j$ and the maximal ideal $I$ of the local ring $B$ (its Jacobson radical) to get $I^j=0$. Thus each inclusion $I^{j+1}\subset I^j$ is strict while $I^j\ne0$. Starting from $I^0=B$ of $K$-dimension $d$, $d$ strict decreases leave dimension at most zero, proving the assertion. This is the dimension-count argument used at the end of Milne 11.32, with Nakayama (Stacks Tag 00DV, lemma-NAK(2)) made explicit.

Use [lem-sfb-finite-group-faithful-regular-matrices] on $C$, and put $U=(u_{ij})\in\operatorname{GL}_d(B)$. Surjectivity of its coordinate map shows that $I$ is generated by $u_{ij}-\delta_{ij}$: the extra generator $\det(U)^{-1}-1=-\det(U)^{-1}(\det(U)-1)$ lies in that ideal too. Since $C$ is commutative, multiplication by $p$ is a group-scheme endomorphism. For $f=[p]^*:B\to B$ the representation identity gives $f(U)=U^p$, so $f(U-1)=U^p-1=(U-1)^p$. The last power is a MATRIX power: its entries are sums of products of $p$ entries of $U-1$, hence lie in $I^p$. Therefore $f(I)\subseteq I^p$. Inductively $f^s(I)\subseteq I^{p^s}$: it is tautological at $s=0$, and applying $f$ to $I^{p^s}$ gives a subideal of $(I^p)^{p^s}=I^{p^{s+1}}$. For $s=r$ this is zero by Step 5. The composite $f^r=[p^r]^*=[d]^*$ is the identity on $K$ and kills $I$, hence sends every $b$ to $\epsilon(b)1$. This is exactly the coordinate map of the zero homomorphism of $C$, so $[d]=0$.

In both characteristic cases, $[d]=0$ on $C$ and $[q]=0$ on $H_K$. Since $n=dq$, the $n$-fold sum is zero on each factor of $G\simeq C\times_KH_K$ and therefore on $G_K$. The coordinate-map injectivity of Step 1 descends this equality to the original $k$. Evaluating the equality of morphisms on any commutative $k$-algebra $R$ gives $nx=0$ for every $x\in G(R)$. Conversely these pointwise identities include $R=A$ and its universal point $\operatorname{id}_A$, so they imply the equality of the coordinate maps and hence of the scheme morphisms. This proves every clause, including the asserted equivalence.
